title: Pattern Recognition
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Using the chess research of de Groot, Simon and Chase, the author argues that expertise is stored pattern recognition rather than raw intelligence. He applies this to new CEOs, who arrive having mastered one function and now face positions they have never seen. Success in the role comes less from brilliant moves than from avoiding a small set of repeated, expensive mistakes, and few people hold the job long enough to meet them. The move is to recast asking for outside help as chess players use seconds and opening theory, rather than as an admission that someone is smarter. A fictional talent review shows how an experienced eye spots an implausible count of weak performers. The essay ends by promoting the author's own CEO operating system and tool.
points: Chess masters excel because they recognize familiar positions in chunks, not because of better memory.
New CEOs bring patterns from a prior function that mostly do not apply to the new job.
CEO success depends more on avoiding a handful of common mistakes than on brilliant moves.
The same traps recur, though each CEO believes their situation is unique.
The useful question to ask is who has seen this before, not who is smarter.
quotes: The masters’ edge came from somewhere else. They had seen positions like the real one thousands of times, and they read it in chunks: the castled king behind its wall of pawns, the bishop on the long diagonal, the knight on its usual square.
Most new CEOs sense that the job is different. What they miss is that the difference comes down to patterns.
The job has an unusual property. CEOs who succeed tend to do it less by making brilliant moves than by avoiding bad ones.

The traps repeat more than most CEOs think. Nearly every CEO I’ve worked with is convinced their situation is unique: their industry is different, their board is different, their people are different.
An executive runs his department under a side deal with the previous CEO. The leadership team agrees in the meeting and does something else afterward.
You can be brilliant and still never get enough repetitions in one seat to learn the patterns.
So the next time you’re inclined to work through something alone because nobody you could call is smarter than you, it’s worth asking a different question: who has seen this before?
